names.en: Treaty of Shimonoseki cedes Taiwan to Japan

card.en: Under Article 2 of the treaty that ended the First Sino-Japanese War, the Qing court ceded Taiwan and the Penghu islands to Japan. Taiwan's residents, including indigenous peoples who held most of the mountain areas, were not parties to it.

indigenous_thread: Much of the interior was not under effective Qing administration in 1895; the treaty transferred a claim, not control.
notes: Vocabulary: 'cession' (treaty term). Check 'not effective control' phrasing against Barclay before publish.

date_note: Proclaimed May 1895; collapsed by October 1895 (exact dates to confirm)

card.en: A short-lived republic proclaimed by Qing officials and local elites in opposition to the cession. It collapsed within months as Japanese forces advanced south. Historians debate how far it was a true independence project versus a loyalist stopgap.

notes: Confirm exact dates and the 'loyalist vs independence' debate with a dedicated academic source. Draft. Blueprint Chronology gives 23 May for the proclamation and October for the fall of Tainan (TODO: source both).

card.en: The colonial government surveyed land holdings, clarifying titles and widening the tax base. It also reclassified much upland and forest as state land, which affected indigenous communities.

indigenous_thread: State claim over uplands and forests removed customary hunting and farming territories from indigenous control.
notes: Verify end year and the forest/upland claim with page refs.

names.en: Western trunk railway completed (Keelung to Kaohsiung)

date_note: Construction on Japanese-era sections began in 1899; completion ceremony 1908 (confirm). Earlier Qing line Keelung to Hsinchu built c. 1887-1893.
geometry_note: Schematic: straight segments between approximate modern station locations (Keelung, Taipei, Taoyuan, Hsinchu, Miaoli, Taichung, Changhua, Chiayi, Tainan, Kaohsiung). Not a surveyed alignment.

card.en: The north-south railway linked ports, sugar districts and cities, and moved troops as well as goods. Part of it reused the Qing-era Keelung to Hsinchu line.

notes: Do NOT claim 'first railway in China'. Check Qing segment dates and mileage. Needs line geometry (stations list). Blueprint Sources tab confirms the Keelung to Kaohsiung main line in 1908 and the Qing trains to Taipei (November 1891) and Hsinchu (1893). names.en: Chianan Irrigation System and Wushantou Reservoir
names.zh: 嘉南大圳 / 烏山頭水庫

date_note: Built 1920 to 1930 under engineer Hatta Yoichi (confirm)
geometry_note: Schematic: one stylized canal running north from the Wushantou Reservoir (first point) across the Chianan plain. Not the actual canal network.

card.en: A large irrigation network in the Chianan plain that expanded paddy and sugarcane farming. Its legacy is remembered differently by different communities, including the farmers who paid water fees.

notes: Needs primary or official source and an academic source on costs and burden before use. Blueprint Sources tab lists the Chianan Management Office history as confirming 1920 to 1930; irrigated area is given as 100,000 to 150,000 hectares depending on the source, so no single figure is used. Blueprint card candidate: who built it, with what labor. TODO: academic source on labor and water fees.

names.en: First modern sugar mill opens at Qiaotou

geometry_note: Approximate site in today's Qiaotou District, Kaohsiung.

card.en: The first modern sugar mill on the island opened at Qiaotou, in today's Kaohsiung, in 1902. Sugar, backed by colonial government policy, became Taiwan's main industry in the following decades.

notes: From Blueprint Chronology (1900s) and Sources tab third pass. Charter: say who built it. TODO: name the operating company and its backers from a source. zh name is the modern site name; TODO: confirm the colonial-era name. Japanese-era sugar figures remain unverified; none are used.

card.en: Narrow-gauge railways carrying cane to the mills began operating in April 1908, the same year the western trunk line was completed.

notes: From Blueprint Chronology and Sources tab third pass. TODO: map the network from a sourced historical map; no geometry until then.

names.zh: 臺灣議會設置請願運動

date_note: 15 petitions, 1921 to 1934; the Taiwanese Cultural Association was founded 17 October 1921

card.en: Taiwanese activists sent 15 petitions to the Imperial Diet in Tokyo asking for an elected Taiwanese assembly. All of them failed. The movement still formed a base for Taiwanese political thought.

notes: From Blueprint Chronology (1921 to 1934) and the confirmed-claims table. TODO: name the leading organizers from the Tai Pao-tsun essay; add page refs from a scholarly source. Blueprint card candidate: the 15 petitions that all failed and still mattered.

card.en: Seediq fighters attacked Japanese people at Musha. Colonial forces responded with a large military campaign. A second violent episode against surviving Seediq followed in 1931.

indigenous_thread: Must be told from Seediq perspectives; consult Seediq community and scholars before publish.
notes: Earlier chat flagged wording on chemical weapons; use only a well-sourced, measured statement. Sensitive: consent and review required. Blueprint: the uprising is staged in its own scene with Seediq voices, approved by community advisors; this marker is a placeholder only.

card.en: A Taiwanese-language popular song with music by Teng Yu-hsien and lyrics by Lee Lin-chiu, from the early 1930s. It is a landmark of Taiwanese-language popular music.

notes: Rights: composition by Teng treated as public domain; Lee's lyrics protected in Taiwan to end of 2029 (per Blueprint). Do not display lyrics. Use only a new or licensed recording (see music_tracker.csv). Blueprint: Teng Yu-hsien was a Hakka musician; card candidate: how a Taiwanese-language hit came from a Hakka composer.

date_note: Figures cover the war years; conscription began only in 1945

card.en: About 207,000 Taiwanese served Japan's war effort, roughly 80,000 as soldiers and 127,000 as military employees. By Japan's own figures, about 30,300 were killed or missing. Conscription began only in 1945.

notes: Blueprint Sources tab gives 207,183 served and 30,304 killed or missing; rounded on the card. Vocabulary: 'military employees' (gunzoku); confirm the term with a scholar. zh name is a common term; TODO: review alternatives. Blueprint card candidate: Taiwanese soldiers in Japan's army.

names.en: Myth: 'Japan built modern Taiwan' vs 'Japan only extracted'

card.myth: Colonial rule was either purely beneficial modernization or purely extraction.
card.fact: Infrastructure and public health expanded, and the system was designed to serve imperial and colonial-state interests, with unequal legal and economic treatment. Historians weigh these differently.

notes: Present as an open debate. Add Taiwanese-language scholarship.
